questions.question: What is EIGRP DUAL (Diffusing Update Algorithm)?
options: A loop-free, finite-state machine that finds the best path (Successor) and backup path (Feasible Successor) guaranteeing freedom from routing loops without periodic recalculations
questions.explanation: DUAL runs in EIGRP to select loop-free routes. It maintains the Successor (best path) and Feasible Successors (backup paths meeting FC). Avoids Dijkstra's CPU-intensive SPF calculation while guaranteeing loop-free convergence.

questions.question: What is the difference between OSPF stub, totally stubby, and NSSA areas?
options: Stub: blocks external LSAs (Type 5). Totally stubby: also blocks inter-area LSAs (Type 3). NSSA: like stub but allows limited external route import via Type 7 LSAs — for areas with non-OSPF routing
questions.explanation: Stub area: no Type 5 (external) LSAs, uses default route. Totally stubby (Cisco): no Type 3 or Type 5 LSAs. NSSA: blocks Type 5 but allows redistribution via Type 7 (converted to Type 5 by ABR). Reduces LSDB size.

questions.question: What is BGP route reflection and why is it needed?
options: Solves the iBGP full mesh requirement — a Route Reflector (RR) re-advertises iBGP routes to its clients, eliminating the need for all routers to peer with each other (O(n²) problem)
questions.explanation: iBGP requires full mesh (every router peers with every other). With N routers: N(N-1)/2 sessions. Route Reflectors break this: clients peer only with RR; RR re-advertises routes. Confederations are the alternative solution.

questions.question: What is MPLS Label Distribution Protocol (LDP)?
options: Distributes MPLS labels between neighbor LSRs so that packets can be forwarded based on labels rather than IP lookups throughout the MPLS network
questions.explanation: LDP (or TDP, RSVP-TE for traffic engineering) establishes label-to-FEC (Forwarding Equivalency Class) bindings between Label Switching Routers. Each LSR maintains a Label Information Base (LIB) and forwards packets using label lookup.

questions.question: What is QoS DSCP and how does it relate to IP precedence?
options: DSCP is legacy; IP precedence is modern

DSCP (RFC 2474) uses 6 bits of the DSCP field in the IP header for 64 possible values. IP precedence used 3 bits (8 values). DSCP is backward compatible — EF, AF, CS classes map to IP precedence values
DSCP is only for voice traffic
questions.explanation: DSCP uses 6 bits of the original ToS byte (IP header), allowing 64 PHB (Per-Hop Behavior) values. Expedited Forwarding (EF/46): low latency for voice. Assured Forwarding (AF): guaranteed minimum bandwidth. CS (Class Selector): backward compat with IP Precedence.

questions.question: What is SD-WAN and what problem does it solve?
options: Software-Defined WAN — decouples WAN networking from hardware, enabling centralized policy-based management across multiple WAN transports (MPLS, broadband, LTE) with automatic path selection
questions.explanation: SD-WAN (Cisco Viptela/SDWAN, VMware VeloCloud) centralizes WAN control, enables application-aware routing, automatic failover between WAN links, and reduces costs by using broadband/LTE alongside MPLS.

questions.question: What is VRF (Virtual Routing and Forwarding)?
options: Creates multiple independent routing tables on a single router, allowing overlapping IP address spaces and complete routing isolation between customers or VPNs
questions.explanation: VRF creates virtual routers within a physical router, each with its own routing table, forwarding table, and interfaces. Used in MPLS L3 VPNs (VRF-Lite without MPLS), multi-tenant environments, and network segmentation.

questions.question: What is BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection)?
options: A lightweight, rapid failure detection protocol providing sub-second hello timers to detect link or path failures faster than routing protocol timers
questions.explanation: BFD detects failures in milliseconds vs OSPF/EIGRP hello/dead timers (seconds). BFD sessions run independently, notifying routing protocols when failure detected. Supported by OSPF, EIGRP, BGP, IS-IS, and static routes.

questions.question: What is the purpose of RESTCONF/NETCONF in network automation?
options: NETCONF (XML/SSH, RFC 6241) and RESTCONF (REST/HTTP, RFC 8040) are IETF protocols for programmatic network device configuration and state retrieval — enabling model-driven network automation
questions.explanation: NETCONF uses XML over SSH for transactional configuration management (commit/rollback). RESTCONF uses REST/HTTP with JSON or XML for simpler programmatic access. Both use YANG data models. Foundation of modern network automation.

questions.question: What is Cisco DNA Center and its role in Intent-Based Networking?
options: Cisco's central controller for network automation, providing design, provisioning, assurance, and policy enforcement across the campus network using intent-based networking principles
questions.explanation: Cisco DNA Center uses intent (business requirements) to automatically configure network devices consistently. Provides: network design templates, zero-touch provisioning, AI-driven assurance, policy enforcement via SD-Access.

questions.question: What is OSPF route redistribution and what must be considered?
options: Importing routes from one routing protocol into another — requires setting appropriate metric and administrative distance, potential routing loops must be prevented with filters or route tags
questions.explanation: Redistribution imports routes between protocols (EIGRP↔OSPF, Static↔OSPF). Issues: suboptimal routing, routing loops (two-way redistribution). Mitigations: route tags (mark redistributed routes to prevent re-redistribution), distribute-lists, prefix-lists.

questions.question: What is a GRE tunnel?
options: Generic Routing Encapsulation — encapsulates virtually any Layer 3 protocol inside IP packets, creating a virtual point-to-point tunnel between endpoints across IP networks
questions.explanation: GRE (Protocol 47) wraps packets in an IP + GRE header, allowing non-IP protocols or multicast over IP networks. GRE itself provides no encryption — combine with IPSec for secure tunnels. Used in DMVPN and SD-WAN.

questions.question: What is DMVPN (Dynamic Multipoint VPN)?
options: A Cisco VPN technology that combines GRE tunnels, mGRE, NHRP, and IPSec to enable scalable hub-and-spoke VPNs with dynamic spoke-to-spoke tunnels on demand
questions.explanation: DMVPN phases: Phase 1 (hub-and-spoke, all traffic through hub), Phase 2 (spoke-to-spoke direct tunnels, no summarization), Phase 3 (spoke-to-spoke with summarization via NHRP redirect). Reduces hub load.

questions.question: What is IS-IS and how does it compare to OSPF?
options: IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) is an IGP link-state protocol similar to OSPF but runs directly over Layer 2 (not IP). Preferred by large ISPs. Supports IPv4 and IPv6 natively in the same process
questions.explanation: IS-IS (ISO 10589) is a link-state protocol using Dijkstra like OSPF. Runs at Layer 2 (IP-independent), making it resilient to IP issues. Uses levels instead of areas. Widely used by large ISP backbones (commonly more than OSPF for ISPs).

questions.question: What is PBR (Policy-Based Routing)?
options: Routes traffic based on criteria other than destination IP (source IP, port, protocol, packet size, ToS) — overrides the normal routing table lookup for specified traffic
questions.explanation: PBR uses route-maps applied to interfaces to forward packets based on ACL matches (source, destination, protocol) to specific next-hops. Use cases: route VoIP to MPLS, route HTTP via broadband, load balancing by source.

questions.question: What is Cisco SD-Access and its key components?
options: A campus network architecture using VXLAN fabric with a central overlay control plane (LISP), ISE for policy, DNA Center for management — provides user/device segmentation via SGTs
questions.explanation: SD-Access: Underlay (routed access), Overlay (VXLAN/LISP), Policy (ISE+SGT/SGACLs), Management (DNA Center). Virtual Networks (VNs) provide macro-segmentation; Scalable Group Tags (SGTs) provide micro-segmentation.

questions.question: What is VXLAN and what problem does it solve?
options: Virtual Extensible LAN — encapsulates Layer 2 frames in UDP/IP, extending Layer 2 over Layer 3 networks and overcoming the 4094 VLAN limit (16 million VXLAN segments via 24-bit VNI)
questions.explanation: VXLAN (RFC 7348) uses UDP port 4789 to tunnel Layer 2 frames over IP networks. Solves: 4094 VLAN limit (uses 24-bit VNID = 16M segments), enables Layer 2 adjacency across routed fabrics. Core of modern data center and SD-Access overlays.

questions.question: What is multicast PIM Sparse Mode?
options: Protocol Independent Multicast Sparse Mode — assumes receivers are sparse. Uses a Rendezvous Point (RP) for initial source/receiver discovery; direct source trees built after RPT path established
questions.explanation: PIM-SM (RFC 7761) builds shared trees via RP and source trees (SPT). Receivers join via IGMP; PIM Join messages travel toward RP/source. Cisco uses Auto-RP or PIM BSR for RP discovery. SSM (Source Specific Multicast) avoids RP entirely.

questions.question: What is Cisco IOS-XE, IOS-XR, and NX-OS?
options: Three names for the same software

IOS-XE: modular IOS for enterprise routers/switches (ASR, ISR). IOS-XR: carrier-grade, high-availability OS for service provider routers (ASR 9K, CRS). NX-OS: data center OS for Nexus switches (feature-rich, Linux-based)
questions.explanation: IOS-XE: modular architecture (SPA/SIP separation), enterprise-grade. IOS-XR: microkernel, in-service software upgrade (ISSU), massive scale, 32-bit process separation. NX-OS: Linux-based, programmable, feature-rich for data center.

questions.question: What is Cisco ACI (Application Centric Infrastructure)?
options: A software-defined data center networking solution using APIC controllers, policy-driven automation, and EPG-based segmentation instead of traditional VLAN-based segmentation
questions.explanation: ACI: APIC cluster (3 controllers), Leaf-Spine topology with VXLAN/EVPN overlay. Key concepts: Tenant, VRF, Bridge Domain (BD), Endpoint Group (EPG), Contract (policy). Policy defined in APIC, pushed to spine/leaf hardware.

questions.question: What is EVPN (Ethernet VPN)?
options: RFC 7432 — MP-BGP based control plane for VXLAN and MPLS overlay networks, enabling Layer 2 and Layer 3 VPN services with MAC/IP learning via BGP instead of data plane flooding
questions.explanation: EVPN uses MP-BGP route types (Type 2: MAC/IP, Type 3: Inclusive Multicast, Type 5: IP prefix) as control plane for VXLAN. Replaces flood-and-learn with BGP-based MAC distribution, enabling scalable data center overlays.

questions.question: What is YANG and its role in network automation?
options: Yet Another Next Generation — a data modeling language (RFC 7950) that defines the structure of network device configuration and operational state data consumed by NETCONF and RESTCONF
questions.explanation: YANG models define the schema for network data — what configuration parameters exist, their types, constraints, and relationships. Vendors publish YANG models for their devices. Tools: pyang (validation), netconf-console, nornir, pyATS.

questions.question: What is Ansible in the context of network automation?
options: An agentless automation tool using SSH/NETCONF and YAML playbooks to configure network devices — no agent software needed on managed devices
questions.explanation: Ansible uses playbooks (YAML) with network modules (ios_config, nxos_vlan, etc.) to automate device configuration. Agentless (connects via SSH/NETCONF). Idempotent. Popular modules: ios_command, eos_config, junos_config.

questions.question: What is Python's role in network automation?
options: The dominant programming language for network automation — used with libraries like Netmiko (SSH), NAPALM (multi-vendor), requests (REST APIs), nornir (framework), pyATS (Cisco testing)
questions.explanation: Python + Netmiko: SSH connections to devices. NAPALM: vendor-neutral API for config/state. Nornir: parallel automation framework. pyATS/Genie: Cisco testing framework. Requests: REST API calls to controllers, cloud APIs.

questions.question: What is Spanning Tree PortFast trunk mode and when is it used?
options: PortFast trunk enables rapid transition to forwarding on trunk ports connecting to hypervisors/non-switch devices that won't cause loops — useful for servers with multiple VMs sending BPDUs
Enables PortFast on all switch ports
questions.explanation: Standard PortFast is for access ports. PortFast trunk is for trunk ports connecting to servers/hypervisors that need rapid forwarding without STP delay but aren't switches. Must still avoid connecting to other switches with this setting.

questions.question: What is the purpose of Cisco DNA Assurance?
options: Uses AI/ML to continuously monitor network health, identify anomalies, correlate issues across devices, and provide guided remediation with root cause analysis
questions.explanation: DNA Assurance provides 360° network visibility with AI-driven insights, AI-driven issue detection, client health scores, application performance monitoring, and natural language search for troubleshooting.

questions.question: What is IS-IS Level 1 vs Level 2?
options: Level 1: intra-area routing (like OSPF non-backbone). Level 2: inter-area routing (like OSPF backbone Area 0). L1/L2 routers are ABR equivalents, connecting areas to the L2 backbone
questions.explanation: IS-IS levels: L1 = intra-area (knows only own area topology). L2 = inter-area backbone (knows all area prefixes). L1/L2 = both (like OSPF ABR). All L2 routers form a contiguous backbone. No concept of a 'Area 0' like OSPF.

questions.question: What is the purpose of LISP (Locator/ID Separation Protocol) in SD-Access?
options: Separates endpoint identity (EID — IP/MAC) from its location (RLOC — routing locator) — enables mobility without changing routing tables. Used as overlay control plane in Cisco SD-Access
questions.explanation: LISP maps EIDs to RLOCs via a Map-Server/Map-Resolver. When a host moves, only the LISP map changes, not the routing table. In SD-Access, LISP distributes host-to-switch-location mappings across the fabric.

questions.question: What is MPLS TE (Traffic Engineering)?
options: Extends MPLS to route traffic along explicitly specified paths (LSPs) based on bandwidth constraints and optimization goals, rather than following the IGP shortest path
questions.explanation: MPLS TE uses RSVP-TE to signal explicit LSPs. Routers run OSPF-TE/IS-IS-TE (with TE extensions to share bandwidth info). Offline computation or PCEP/SDN controllers calculate optimal paths. Used for WAN optimization and congestion avoidance.

questions.question: What is Cisco IOS scripting with Tcl and EEM?
options: TCL (Tool Command Language) shell in IOS enables basic scripting. EEM (Embedded Event Manager) allows automated responses to events (syslog, SNMP, CLI, timer) with applet policies or Tcl scripts — no external server needed
questions.explanation: EEM applets are simple IOS policies: 'event syslog pattern [regex]' triggers 'action cli command [cmd]'. EEM Tcl scripts provide more complex logic. Use cases: auto-recovery, correlation, compliance checks, automated troubleshooting.

questions.question: What is NHRP (Next Hop Resolution Protocol)?
options: Maps overlay (tunnel) IP addresses to underlay physical IP addresses in DMVPN — enables spokes to discover each other's physical IP for direct spoke-to-spoke tunnels
questions.explanation: In DMVPN, NHRP allows spoke routers to query the hub for the physical (NBMA) address of other spokes, enabling on-demand spoke-to-spoke tunnels without pre-configuring all pairs. Hub maintains NHRP database.

questions.question: What is Cisco SDA Virtual Network (VN) and Scalable Group Tag (SGT)?
options: VN: macro-segmentation (separate routing domain, like VRF-lite). SGT: 16-bit tag assigned to users/devices by ISE providing micro-segmentation via SGACLs — allows policy based on user role rather than IP
questions.explanation: SD-Access segmentation: VNs (like VRFs) for isolation between major groups (IoT, Guest, Corp). Within a VN, SGTs (1-65535) tag users/endpoints by role. SGACLs (Cisco TrustSec) enforce which SGTs can communicate.

questions.question: What is BGP communities attribute?
options: A well-known or private transitive attribute tagging BGP routes with 32-bit values to influence routing policy across AS boundaries — used for filtering, preference, and route manipulation
questions.explanation: BGP communities: NO_EXPORT (don't advertise beyond AS), NO_ADVERTISE (don't advertise to any peer), LOCAL_AS. Custom communities: 'ip community-list' + route-map to set local-preference, MED, or filter routes based on community tags.

questions.question: What is GETVPN (Group Encrypted Transport VPN)?
options: A Cisco VPN that encrypts traffic within an existing MPLS/WAN network without changing IP headers — group members share encryption keys, maintaining routing/QoS transparency
questions.explanation: GETVPN uses Tunnel-less encryption (preserves original IP headers) via GET VPN with a Key Server (KS) distributing group keys to Group Members (GMs). Traffic encrypted in place on existing MPLS WAN. No tunneling overhead.

questions.question: What is Equal-Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) routing?
options: Load balancing across multiple paths with equal cost metrics — packets distributed across all equal-cost next-hops for a destination. Supported by OSPF, EIGRP, IS-IS, BGP (with policy)
questions.explanation: ECMP: if multiple routes to same destination with equal metric exist, traffic distributed across all (per-destination or per-packet). Default ECMP: 4 paths (IOS), up to 16 configurable. EIGRP supports unequal-cost load balancing (variance command).

questions.question: What is the purpose of AS Path prepending in BGP?
options: Shortens the AS path for faster routing
Makes a route less preferred by artificially lengthening the AS path attribute — used to influence inbound traffic when multihomed to multiple ISPs
Removes AS numbers from the path
questions.explanation: AS path prepending adds your ASN multiple times to the AS_PATH of routes advertised to specific ISPs. Longer AS path = less preferred. Used for inbound traffic engineering: prefer ISP-A over ISP-B by prepending on ISP-B advertisements.

questions.question: What is Cisco's Trustworthy Systems initiative and Network Security?
options: Hardware Root of Trust, Secure Boot, code signing, SUDI (Secure Unique Device Identity) certificates, and TAm (Trust Anchor Module) ensuring Cisco devices boot trusted code and can be cryptographically identified
questions.explanation: Cisco Trustworthy Systems: TAm/SUDI chips provide hardware identity. Secure Boot verifies IOS code signatures. ACT2 (Anti-Counterfeiting Technology 2) prevents fake hardware. Network operators can verify device authenticity cryptographically.

questions.question: What is a network fabric in modern data center design?
options: A highly scalable Leaf-Spine topology where every leaf connects to every spine, providing equal-cost multi-path routing, predictable latency, and easy horizontal scaling
questions.explanation: Leaf-Spine fabric: every leaf switch connects to every spine switch (no leaf-to-leaf or spine-to-spine connections). Benefits: any-to-any East-West traffic in 2 hops, ECMP across all spines, add capacity by adding leaf+spine pairs.

questions.question: What is Model-Driven Telemetry (MDT) vs SNMP polling?
options: MDT: devices push operational data to collectors at high frequency using streaming (gRPC/gNMI) — real-time, scalable. SNMP polling: manager requests data periodically — limited frequency, doesn't scale for modern networks
questions.explanation: MDT streams data in real-time using gRPC/gNMI with YANG models — sub-second updates possible. SNMP GET polls every 5+ minutes. MDT used with InfluxDB/Grafana, Prometheus, or vendor platforms for real-time network observability.

questions.question: What is Cisco NSO (Network Services Orchestrator)?
options: A network automation and orchestration platform using YANG models and NEDs (Network Element Drivers) to provide service lifecycle management across multi-vendor networks via a single API
questions.explanation: NSO uses YANG models + NEDs (vendor-specific drivers) to provide a vendor-neutral abstraction. Services (VPNs, VLAN configs) modeled once, NSO translates to vendor-specific CLI/NETCONF. Supports rollback, dry-run, compliance.

questions.question: What is the purpose of OSPF LSA Type 3 (Summary LSA)?
options: Generated by ABRs to advertise network prefixes from one area to other areas — allows inter-area routing while limiting full LSDB propagation across areas
questions.explanation: Type 3 LSAs are generated by ABRs, summarizing networks from non-backbone areas into Area 0 and vice versa. They don't carry the full topology — just the prefix and cost, keeping LSDB smaller in remote areas.

questions.question: What is EIGRP named mode and its advantages?
options: A modern EIGRP configuration mode (vs classic mode) providing: named instances, IPv4/IPv6 unified config, wide metrics (64-bit), per-AF timers, and simplified configuration under 'router eigrp [name]'
questions.explanation: Named EIGRP: 'router eigrp NAME' with address-family sections. Wide metrics use 64-bit composite (supports >100Gbps links properly). Backward compatible. All new EIGRP configurations should use named mode.

questions.question: What is BGP Weight attribute and how does it differ from Local Preference?
options: Weight: Cisco-proprietary, local to the router only (not advertised to peers), influences outbound path selection per-router. Local Preference: advertised within iBGP AS, influences all routers in the AS for outbound path choice
questions.explanation: BGP path selection: Weight > Local Preference > Locally originated > AS Path > Origin > MED > eBGP > IGP metric > oldest > Router ID. Weight: 0-65535, local only. Local Preference: 0-4294967295, AS-wide, higher = preferred.

questions.question: What is VPLS (Virtual Private LAN Service)?
options: An MPLS/IP service providing multipoint Layer 2 Ethernet bridging across a provider network — connects multiple sites in a single broadcast domain as if directly connected on the same LAN
questions.explanation: VPLS creates a distributed virtual switch across provider MPLS network. All customer sites appear in same L2 domain. Uses PWs (pseudowires) between PE routers. Replaced increasingly by EVPN which provides the same service more efficiently.

questions.question: What is QoS WRED (Weighted Random Early Detection)?
options: A congestion avoidance mechanism that randomly drops packets before queue fills based on DSCP/IP precedence marking — prevents TCP global synchronization by causing individual flows to back off at different times
questions.explanation: WRED profiles: min-threshold, max-threshold, drop probability. Between min/max: random drops proportional to congestion. Above max: drop all. Different profiles per DSCP class. Prevents tail-drop TCP sync where all TCP flows simultaneously reduce rate.

questions.question: What is Cisco Catalyst Center (formerly DNA Center) vs traditional CLI management?
options: Catalyst Center: intent-based, policy-driven, REST API, automated provisioning, AI assurance, single pane of glass. CLI: device-by-device, manual, error-prone at scale, no correlation — manages hundreds of devices vs thousands
questions.explanation: Catalyst Center provides: Design (site hierarchy, templates), Policy (SGT-based via ISE), Provision (zero-touch PnP), Assurance (AI health scores, root cause). REST/RESTCONF APIs. Replaces manual CLI for enterprise scale.

questions.question: What is Cisco IOS XE on-box Python scripting?
options: IOS XE supports embedded Python 3 via 'guestshell' Linux container — scripts can call NETCONF/RESTCONF, read EEM events, or use pyATS libraries for on-box network automation without external servers
questions.explanation: IOS XE guestshell: Linux container with Python 3, pip. Can import CLI outputs via subprocess, use NETCONF to the local device, respond to EEM events. Scripts run directly on the device — no controller needed for simple automation.

questions.question: What is OSPF SPF (Shortest Path First) algorithm and when does it run?
options: Dijkstra's SPF algorithm calculates the shortest path tree from the router itself to all destinations using the LSDB. Triggers: topology change (new LSA), timer expiry. Incremental SPF for less disruptive minor changes
questions.explanation: Full SPF: computationally expensive, triggered by Type 1/2 LSA changes (topology). Partial Route Calculation (PRC): less expensive, triggered by Type 3-7 LSA changes (prefix changes). SPF timers: initial delay + incremental backoff prevent oscillation.

questions.question: What is MPLS PHP (Penultimate Hop Popping)?
options: The penultimate (second-to-last) LSR pops the MPLS label before forwarding to the egress LSR — reduces double lookup at egress: no MPLS lookup + IP lookup. Egress receives native IP or single label
questions.explanation: PHP: implicit null label (3) signals penultimate router to pop. Egress LSR does only IP lookup, not MPLS+IP. Ultimate Hop Popping (UHP): explicit null label (0) — label kept until egress for QoS or tracking purposes.

questions.question: What is Segment Routing (SR)?
options: A source-routing paradigm where the ingress router programs the packet path using a stack of segment IDs (SIDs) in the header — eliminates need for per-flow state in core (RSVP-TE, LDP)
questions.explanation: SR-MPLS: SIDs encoded as MPLS labels. SR-v6: SIDs in IPv6 header extension. Topology learned via IGP extensions (OSPF-SR, IS-IS-SR). Benefits: source routing, traffic engineering without per-flow signaling, ECMP, fast reroute.

questions.question: What is NSF/SSO (Non-Stop Forwarding/Stateful Switchover) in Cisco platforms?
options: SSO: active/standby RP (Route Processor) synchronize state continuously. Failover: standby takes over in milliseconds, maintains hardware forwarding. NSF: continues forwarding during routing protocol reconvergence using stale routes
questions.explanation: Without NSF/SSO: RP failure = routing restart = traffic loss during convergence. With SSO: standby RP fully synchronized, sub-second failover. With NSF: keeps forwarding during reconvergence. OSPF/BGP/EIGRP-aware NSF helpers exist.

questions.question: What is the purpose of route redistribution metric in OSPF?
options: When redistributing into OSPF, you must set a seed metric — default external metric is 20 (E2 type, cost doesn't increase hop-by-hop). E1 type: cost accumulates as packets traverse OSPF topology
questions.explanation: OSPF external types: E2 (default): constant metric end-to-end, cost = external metric only. E1: metric increases by OSPF cost of path to ASBR + external metric. E1 preferred over E2 if both exist for same prefix.

questions.question: What is Cisco SD-WAN vManage/vSmart/vBond architecture?
options: Three names for the same device

vManage: management plane (GUI, API, policy config). vSmart: control plane (OMP routing protocol, policy distribution). vBond: orchestration plane (initial authentication, NAT traversal for WAN edges)
questions.explanation: SD-WAN planes: Management (vManage: telemetry, templates, policies), Control (vSmart: OMP routes, policy enforcement, key distribution), Data (vEdge/cEdge: IPsec tunnels, forwarding), Orchestration (vBond: initial device onboarding, NAT discovery).

questions.question: What is LISP map caching and why does it matter for performance?
options: LISP routers cache EID-to-RLOC mappings locally after first lookup — subsequent packets to same EID are encapsulated without querying Map-Server again. Cache TTL: default 24 hours
questions.explanation: LISP first packet: ITR sends Map-Request to Map-Resolver → Map-Server → responds with RLOC. ITR caches EID→RLOC mapping. Subsequent packets: encapsulate directly using cached RLOC. Map-Cache: show lisp site / show lisp map-cache.

questions.question: What is Cisco TrustSec and SGT propagation?
options: SGTs (Scalable Group Tags) are 16-bit values assigned to endpoints by ISE on authentication, then propagated by Cisco switches inline (802.1AE MACsec tag) or out-of-band (SGT Exchange Protocol / SXP for non-SGT switches)
questions.explanation: TrustSec propagation: Inline tagging (hardware support, L2 tag preserved hop-to-hop), SXP (software protocol mapping SGT to IP for non-TrustSec devices). SGACLs enforced at egress switch or ASA/FTD based on source/destination SGT pair.

questions.question: What is MPLS L3VPN and how are customer routes kept separate?
options: Customer VRFs on PE routers hold separate routing tables per customer. MP-BGP with VPNv4 address family carries customer routes between PEs with RT (Route Target) communities distinguishing VPNs — core P routers only see MPLS labels
questions.explanation: MPLS L3VPN: CE connects to PE (eBGP/static/OSPF). PE imports routes into VRF, redistributes into MP-BGP VPNv4. RT import/export controls which VPNs receive which routes. P routers: no customer routes, only label forwarding. Two labels: outer (LSP) + inner (VRF).

questions.question: What is NETCONF transaction and why is it superior to CLI for automation?
options: NETCONF provides: atomic transactions (commit or rollback all), candidate configuration (test before commit), lock (exclusive edit access), structured XML data (parseable), error detection — CLI is line-by-line with no transaction guarantee
questions.explanation: NETCONF operations: get-config, edit-config (merge/replace/create/delete), commit, lock/unlock, validate. Candidate datastore: edit without affecting running config, then commit atomically. On error: automatic rollback. Critical for safe automation.

questions.question: What is OSPF area border router (ABR) behavior with multiple areas?
options: ABR advertises all LSA types everywhere
ABR maintains separate LSDB per area, runs SPF per area, generates Type 3 Summary LSAs to advertise prefixes between areas. Summary routes can be configured to reduce inter-area LSA count
questions.explanation: ABR: interface in Area 0 + at least one other area. Separate LSDB per area. Generates Type 3 LSAs from intra-area prefixes. Can summarize: 'area X range prefix mask' reduces Type 3 LSAs. Prevents discontiguous areas via virtual-link.

questions.question: What is Cisco Flexible NetFlow?
options: Collects granular IP flow statistics (source/dest IP, port, protocol, ToS, interface, timestamps) configurable per field — used for network visibility, security anomaly detection, capacity planning, and billing
questions.explanation: Flexible NetFlow: flow record (define keys + non-key fields), flow exporter (IPFIX/NetFlow v9 to collector), flow monitor (combines record + exporter, applied to interface). Collectors: SolarWinds, PRTG, ntopng, ELK stack.

questions.question: What is the purpose of EIGRP Stub routing?
options: Configures a hub-and-spoke spoke router to not advertise routes it learns from the hub back to the hub — prevents spoke-to-spoke routing through hub, reduces query scope, faster convergence
questions.explanation: EIGRP stub router (spoke): 'eigrp stub connected summary'. Hub won't send Queries to stub routers (can't be used as transit). Reduces query domain scope dramatically in large hub-and-spoke topologies, preventing SIA (Stuck In Active) scenarios.

questions.question: What is Cisco ACI Microsegmentation (uSeg)?
options: Extends EPG membership based on VM attributes (IP, MAC, VM name, OS, tag) regardless of port/VLAN — allows policy enforcement at individual VM granularity without changing network topology
questions.explanation: uSeg (microsegmentation) EPGs: endpoints automatically assigned based on attributes learned from VMware vCenter, Kubernetes, or IP/MAC criteria. Same physical network, policy enforced per-VM based on identity, not location.

questions.question: What is an OSPF virtual link and when is it needed?
options: Connects a non-backbone area to Area 0 through a transit area when direct connection isn't possible — temporary fix for discontiguous backbone or area that can't directly connect to Area 0
questions.explanation: Virtual link: configured between two ABRs across a transit area. Makes the non-connected area appear directly connected to Area 0. Not recommended for permanent designs — indicates poor topology. Transit area must not be stub/NSSA.

questions.question: What is IP SLA in Cisco IOS?
options: Active measurement tool generating synthetic traffic (ICMP echo, UDP jitter, HTTP, DNS) to measure network performance (latency, jitter, packet loss) — used for troubleshooting, routing decisions via object tracking, and SLA verification
questions.explanation: IP SLA: 'ip sla 1' define operation (icmp-echo, udp-jitter). 'ip sla schedule'. 'show ip sla statistics'. Track SLA with 'track 1 ip sla 1 reachability' → use in routing: 'ip route ... track 1' (floating static based on reachability).

questions.question: What is Cisco PfRv3 (Performance Routing) in IWAN?
options: Path control technology choosing the best WAN path per-application based on real-time performance metrics (latency, jitter, loss, MOS) — predecessor to SD-WAN application-aware routing
questions.explanation: PfRv3/IWAN: master controller monitors path performance via IP SLA probes, moves traffic between MPLS/broadband based on policy thresholds per application class. Replaced by Cisco SD-WAN (Viptela) which does the same more elegantly.

questions.question: What is the BGP MED (Multi-Exit Discriminator) attribute and how is it used?
options: Suggests preferred entry point into an AS to external peers — lower MED preferred. Only compared between routes from same neighboring AS (by default). Used to influence inbound traffic from a specific neighbor
questions.explanation: MED (metric): advertised to eBGP peers to suggest preferred ingress point. Lower = preferred. Default: compare MED only from same AS ('bgp always-compare-med' to compare across all ASes, but creates routing instability risk). Set with route-map 'set metric'.

questions.question: What is EVPN Type 2 and Type 5 route?
options: Type 2 (MAC/IP Advertisement): advertises learned MAC+IP pairs — used for L2 VPN MAC learning over BGP control plane. Type 5 (IP Prefix): advertises IP prefixes — used for L3 VPN inter-subnet routing in VXLAN/EVPN fabrics
questions.explanation: EVPN Route Types: 1 (Ethernet Auto-Discovery: multi-homing), 2 (MAC/IP: L2 forwarding), 3 (Inclusive Multicast: BUM traffic), 4 (ES Route: multi-homing redundancy), 5 (IP Prefix: L3 routing). Type 2+5 most common in data center fabrics.

questions.question: What is OSPF Graceful Restart (RFC 3623)?
options: Allows an OSPF router undergoing a restart (software upgrade/RP failover) to continue forwarding traffic while rebuilding LSDB — neighbor routers act as 'helpers' maintaining adjacency during restart window
questions.explanation: Graceful restart: restarting router signals helpers via Grace LSA. Helpers maintain adjacency and don't originate topology changes during grace period (default 120s). Allows ISSU (In-Service Software Upgrade) without dropping OSPF routes.

questions.question: What is network function virtualization (NFV)?
options: Replacing dedicated hardware network appliances (firewalls, load balancers, WAN optimizers, IDS) with software running on standard x86 servers — reduces hardware costs, speeds deployment, improves flexibility
questions.explanation: NFV decouples network functions from hardware: virtual firewall (ASAv, Palo Alto VM), virtual router (CSR1000V, vMX), virtual load balancer (F5 BIG-IP VE). Managed via NFVO (NFV Orchestrator) like Cisco NSO or OpenStack Tacker.

questions.question: What is PBR with IP SLA for WAN failover?
options: Using Policy-Based Routing combined with IP SLA object tracking: primary path selected by PBR based on SLA reachability — when SLA probe fails, PBR route-map uses secondary path without changing routing table
questions.explanation: Example: PBR route-map matches HTTP traffic, sets next-hop to MPLS if SLA probe up, internet if down. 'set ip next-hop verify-availability [IP] [seq] track [obj]'. Multiple next-hops tried in order until verified reachable.

questions.question: What is MPLS LDP session protection?
options: Maintains targeted LDP sessions (backup) between routers even when direct link fails — allows LDP session to persist via alternate path, speeding label convergence when primary link restores
questions.explanation: LDP session protection: configure targeted LDP sessions between routers in addition to link-local LDP. If direct link fails, targeted session maintains LDP bindings via alternate path. Dramatically reduces convergence time when link restores.

questions.question: What is Cisco NSF/GR (Graceful Restart) for BGP?
options: Allows a BGP speaker to continue forwarding during BGP restart — restarting router signals restart in OPEN message, helper peers mark routes as stale but continue forwarding during restart timer
questions.explanation: BGP GR: restart timer (default 120s). Restarting router maintains forwarding. Helper peers retain stale routes during graceful restart period. After restart, routes re-advertised and stale routes removed. Critical for hitless ISSU on BGP routers.

questions.question: What is the Cisco 3-tier vs 2-tier campus design?
options: 3-tier: Core (high-speed backbone) + Distribution (routing, policy, aggregation) + Access (endpoints). 2-tier (collapsed core): Distribution+Core merged into single layer — simpler, cheaper for smaller campuses with fewer buildings
questions.explanation: 3-tier: Core (campus backbone, high-speed, no policy), Distribution (routing, ACL, STP, redundancy per building), Access (PoE, VLANs, 802.1X). 2-tier: eliminate separate core for smaller designs. Modern: spine-leaf replacing 3-tier in many designs.

questions.question: What is Cisco IOS EEM TCL vs Applet?
options: Applet: simple inline policy in IOS config (event + ordered actions, limited logic). TCL script: full programming language with conditionals, loops, string manipulation, can import CLI outputs and call NETCONF — much more powerful but requires separate script files
questions.explanation: EEM applet: 'event manager applet NAME / event syslog pattern / action 1.0 cli command'. Good for simple triggered responses. EEM TCL: register_event, event_reqinfo, full TCL logic. TCL scripts stored in flash or TFTP server. Use applet for simple, TCL for complex automation.

questions.question: What is HSRP preemption and its implications?
options: Preemption allows a router with higher priority to take over as Active even if another router is currently Active — must be explicitly enabled with 'standby X preempt'. Without preempt, current Active stays even after higher-priority router recovers
questions.explanation: HSRP preempt: 'standby 1 preempt delay minimum 60' — delay prevents preemption during routing convergence after reboot. Without preempt: current Active stays until it fails. Best practice: enable preempt + delay on primary router to ensure deterministic active placement.

questions.question: What is Cisco IOS-XE YANG data model for interface configuration?
options: Cisco-IOS-XE-native YANG model defines structured interface config (Cisco-IOS-XE-native:interfaces/interface). Standard models: openconfig-interfaces, ietf-interfaces (RFC 7223). NETCONF/RESTCONF clients use these models to read/write config programmatically
questions.explanation: YANG tree for interface: name, type, enabled, ipv4/ipv6 addresses, MTU, description. Accessed via NETCONF get-config/edit-config or RESTCONF GET/PUT/PATCH. 'show yang modules' lists all supported YANG models on device.

questions.question: What is Cisco SD-Access Macro and Micro-Segmentation difference?
options: Macro-segmentation: Virtual Networks (VNs/VRFs) provide complete routing isolation between major groups (corporate, IoT, guest). Micro-segmentation: SGT-based policies within a VN control which user roles can communicate with which resources
questions.explanation: SD-Access layers: VN (VRF-based, L3 isolation, separate routing table per VN) = macro. SGT (16-bit tag assigned by ISE) = micro. SGACLs: 'permit/deny' between source SGT and destination SGT. Both can coexist — VN isolation + fine-grained role policy within VN.

questions.question: What is GRE over IPSec vs IPSec tunnel mode?
options: GRE over IPSec: GRE provides tunnel interface (routing, multicast, any protocol), IPSec provides encryption. IPSec tunnel mode: encrypts IP packet directly (no GRE), no routing protocol support, no multicast. GRE+IPSec needed for dynamic routing over VPN
questions.explanation: IPSec transport mode: encrypts payload, original IP header preserved. IPSec tunnel mode: encrypts entire IP packet, new IP header added. GRE+IPSec: GRE creates tunnel interface for routing/multicast, IPSec encrypts GRE packets. Most enterprise VPNs use GRE+IPSec.

questions.question: What is OSPF SPF timers and why are they important?
options: SPF timers control delay between topology change and SPF calculation: initial delay + incremental backoff (exponential) + max wait. Prevents route flapping from triggering excessive SPF recalculations during instability
questions.explanation: 'timers throttle spf [initial] [min-between] [max-wait]' in ms. Default: 50ms/200ms/5000ms. During flapping: first SPF fast (50ms), subsequent SPFs progressively slower up to 5s — prevents CPU exhaustion during network instability. LSA throttle timers similarly.

questions.question: What is the purpose of BFD Micro-BFD for LAG/LACP?
options: Runs BFD sessions on each member link of a LAG (Link Aggregation Group) — detects individual member link failures faster than LACP timers, allowing rapid removal of failed members from the bundle
questions.explanation: Micro-BFD: per-member-link BFD sessions aggregate into LAG BFD session. If any member BFD session fails, that link removed from LAG immediately. Standard LACP slow timers (30s/90s) = too slow for <1s failure detection. Micro-BFD: millisecond detection.

questions.question: What is Cisco APIC-EM vs Catalyst Center (DNA Center)?
options: APIC-EM: legacy network controller (path trace, ACL analysis, EasyQoS). DNA Center: next-generation platform replacing APIC-EM with SD-Access, AI assurance, intent-based networking, full lifecycle management. APIC-EM EOL 2019
questions.explanation: APIC-EM (Application Policy Infrastructure Controller — Enterprise Module): REST-based path analysis, device discovery. DNA Center/Catalyst Center: full SD-Access controller, AI-powered assurance, automated provisioning, PnP, comprehensive APIs. Major architectural upgrade.

questions.question: What is Cisco Nexus vPC (virtual Port Channel)?
options: Allows two Nexus switches to present themselves as a single logical switch to a downstream device — downstream device forms LAG to both Nexus switches simultaneously, eliminating STP blocked ports and providing active-active uplinks
questions.explanation: vPC: peer keepalive link (management network, detects peer failure), peer link (sync MAC/ARP tables, carry orphan traffic). Downstream device sees one logical switch. Both uplinks active (unlike traditional STP blocking). Critical for ToR switch design.

questions.question: What is BGP confederation?
options: An alternative to route reflectors for solving iBGP full mesh — splits a large AS into smaller sub-ASes (confederation member ASes) that use eBGP between them but appear as a single AS to external peers
questions.explanation: Confederation: AS 65000 split into sub-ASes 65001, 65002. Internal sub-ASes use eBGP between them (path selection with eBGP rules) but AS_PATH shows only outer AS 65000 to external peers. More complex than route reflectors but preserves eBGP semantics.

questions.question: What is RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure) in BGP?
options: Cryptographically validates that BGP route announcements originate from the legitimate owner of the IP prefix — prevents route hijacking via ROA (Route Origin Authorization) records stored in RPKI repositories
questions.explanation: RPKI: prefix owner creates ROA (prefix, origin AS, max prefix length) signed by RIR (ARIN, RIPE). BGP routers validate announcements against RPKI validator — Invalid routes rejected/de-preferred. Critical defense against BGP hijacking (like AS 7007, Pakistan Telecom incidents).

questions.question: What is VXLAN BGP EVPN control plane vs flood-and-learn?
options: Flood-and-learn: BUM (Broadcast, Unknown, Multicast) traffic flooded to all VTEPs for MAC learning — scales poorly. BGP EVPN: MAC/IP learned via BGP Type 2 routes, no flooding needed for unicast — scales to thousands of VTEPs
questions.explanation: Flood-and-learn VXLAN: first packet flooded via multicast or head-end replication. EVPN control plane: VTEPs advertise learned MAC/IP via BGP Type 2 routes before traffic arrives — known unicast forwarding, no flooding for unicast. Critical for scale.

questions.question: What is the purpose of OSPF database exchange process (ExStart/Exchange/Loading)?
options: After 2-Way state: ExStart (elect Master/Slave via higher Router ID), Exchange (exchange DBDs — LSDB summaries), Loading (request missing LSAs via LSR → receive LSU → send LSAck), Full (complete adjacency)
questions.explanation: OSPF neighbor states: Down→Attempt→Init→2-Way→ExStart→Exchange→Loading→Full. ExStart: bidirectional communication confirmed, elect Master (sends DBDs first). Exchange: compare LSDBs via DBDs. Loading: request missing LSAs. Full: synced LSDBs, adjacency complete.

questions.question: What is MPLS-TE explicit path and CSPF?
options: Explicit path: manually defined sequence of nodes for LSP. CSPF (Constrained SPF): modified Dijkstra that considers bandwidth constraints and TE attributes from IGP-TE extensions to calculate optimal path meeting QoS requirements
questions.explanation: MPLS-TE: IGP-TE extensions (OSPF-TE/IS-IS-TE) flood bandwidth availability. CSPF calculates path satisfying constraint (e.g., reserve 100Mbps). RSVP-TE signals LSP along calculated path, reserving bandwidth at each hop. Auto-bandwidth adjusts reservations dynamically.

questions.question: What is Cisco MACsec (802.1AE) and where is it used?
options: IEEE 802.1AE — provides wire-speed hop-by-hop Layer 2 encryption and authentication for Ethernet — encrypts data between directly connected devices (switch-to-switch, switch-to-server) with 128/256-bit AES-GCM
questions.explanation: MACsec: encrypts each Ethernet frame between adjacent devices. Use cases: campus distribution-to-core, switch-to-server links. MKA (MACsec Key Agreement) handles key exchange via 802.1X. Different from IPSec (L3) or TLS (L7) — provides L2 encryption.

questions.question: What is Cisco SD-Access wireless integration?
options: SD-Access extends fabric to wireless: WLCs operate in SD-Access mode, APs are fabric-mode, wireless clients get SGTs assigned by ISE on association — same policy enforcement as wired clients, VXLAN tunnel from AP to fabric edge
questions.explanation: SD-Access wireless: Fabric-enabled WLC, fabric-mode APs (AP acts as VXLAN VTEP or tunnels to fabric edge). Client: connects to SSID → WLC assigns VLAN/VN/SGT via ISE → traffic enters fabric → same policy as wired. Seamless roaming within fabric.

questions.question: What is Cisco NSO service model and service creation?
options: NSO services: YANG service model defines input parameters (customer name, VPN ID, CE-PE links). NSO maps service model to device config via templates/code (Python/Java). Service commit: all device changes atomic — single NSO transaction across all devices
questions.explanation: NSO service lifecycle: service create (calculate device config from service parameters), re-deploy (reconcile after out-of-band changes), delete (remove all device config created by service). Service intent tracked — NSO knows what config it owns.

questions.question: What is the purpose of BGP route dampening?
options: Suppresses unstable (flapping) BGP routes to prevent constant BGP updates from propagating through the internet — a route accumulates penalty with each flap; when penalty exceeds suppress limit, route suppressed until it stabilizes
questions.explanation: BGP dampening: half-life (how fast penalty decays), reuse threshold (when to re-advertise suppressed route), suppress limit (when to suppress), max-suppress-time. Now discouraged for iBGP and most eBGP (RFC 7196) — causes excessive suppression of valid routes.

questions.question: What is EIGRP Unequal-Cost Load Balancing?
options: Uses the 'variance' multiplier: routes with metrics up to variance*FeasibleDistance are installed in routing table and used for load balancing — proportional to inverse of metric (higher metric = less traffic)
Sends all traffic on best path
questions.explanation: EIGRP variance: 'variance 2' means install routes with metric up to 2x Successor metric (must meet Feasibility Condition). Traffic proportional: route with metric 1000 gets 2x traffic of route with metric 2000. Unique EIGRP feature — OSPF only supports ECMP.

questions.question: What is OSPF Fast Convergence with BFD and Link-Down detection?
options: OSPF convergence: link-down detected (BFD: milliseconds, or interface down event: sub-second) → SPF scheduled (throttle timer) → SPF runs → RIB updated → CEF updated. BFD replaces hello timers (default dead: 40s) for fast failure detection
BFD is not compatible with OSPF
questions.explanation: Convergence chain: failure detection (BFD 50ms vs OSPF dead timer 40s) → LSA flood → SPF calc (throttled: 50ms initial) → RIB update → CEF update. With BFD: sub-second. Without: 40s dead timer + SPF + FIB update = 40+ seconds.

questions.question: What is a Cisco Catalyst switch stackwise vs VSS vs vPC?
options: Stackwise (3750/3850/9300): physical stacking cable, true single switch, shared backplane. VSS (4500/6500): two chassis appear as one, single management plane. vPC (Nexus): two independent switches with virtual LAG — still two management planes
questions.explanation: Stackwise: physical ring cable, 80Gbps backplane, 9 switches max, single management IP. VSS: active/standby supervisor, full mesh between chassis, geographic separation possible. vPC: most complex, fully independent management, data center focused.

questions.question: What is PIM Anycast RP?
options: Deploys multiple Rendezvous Point routers with same IP address advertised from multiple locations — sources/receivers find nearest RP via routing; RPs synchronize using MSDP or PIM anycast RP mechanism for source state sharing
questions.explanation: Anycast RP: multiple PEs advertise same RP address. Sources/receivers join nearest RP. RPs share source state via MSDP (SA messages) or native Anycast RP (PIM Register). Provides RP redundancy and load distribution without VRRP.

questions.question: What is the OSPF default-information originate command?
options: Creates a default route in OSPF
Redistributes a default route (0.0.0.0/0) from the routing table into OSPF as a Type 5 External LSA — adds 'always' keyword to originate even without a default route in the routing table
questions.explanation: 'default-information originate': router must have 0.0.0.0/0 in routing table (from static or ISP). 'always': originates regardless. 'metric': sets external metric. 'metric-type 1 or 2': E1 accumulates cost, E2 does not. Common at Internet edge.

questions.question: What is CDP vs LLDP security risk and mitigation?
options: CDP/LLDP advertise: device platform, IOS version, IP addresses, interface info — valuable for attackers doing network reconnaissance. Mitigation: disable on external-facing interfaces ('no cdp enable' per interface), enable only on trusted internal ports
questions.explanation: CDP leak: attacker learns switch model (exploitable vulnerabilities), IOS version, management IP. LLDP has same risk. Best practice: 'no cdp enable' + 'no lldp transmit' + 'no lldp receive' on DMZ/external/user-facing ports. Keep enabled on trunk/uplink ports for topology management.

questions.question: What is OSPF prefix suppression?
options: Prevents a router's transit interfaces (point-to-point links, loopbacks used only for routing) from being advertised into OSPF — reduces LSDB size, prevents exposing infrastructure IP addresses to potential attackers
questions.explanation: 'ip ospf prefix-suppression' per-interface or globally. Transit p2p links: no need to advertise /30 or /31 prefix since hosts never need to reach those IPs directly. Reduces LSDB, hides infrastructure topology. Don't suppress loopbacks used for management.

questions.question: What is BGP route reflection cluster ID?
options: Identifies a cluster of route reflectors — clients only reflect to clients in same cluster. Multiple RRs in same cluster share same cluster-id to prevent routing loops. Loop prevention: CLUSTER_LIST attribute checked for own cluster-id
questions.explanation: RR cluster: one or more RRs serving a set of clients. Cluster-ID in CLUSTER_LIST prevents loops between RRs. Best practice: multiple RRs per cluster for redundancy. Clients peer with all RRs in cluster. RRs in different clusters exchange routes directly.

questions.question: What is In-Service Software Upgrade (ISSU) and what does it require?
options: Upgrades IOS software on a device while maintaining traffic forwarding and protocol adjacencies — requires: redundant supervisor/RP (SSO capable), NSF-aware protocols, hardware support, and same software version on both RPs before upgrade
questions.explanation: ISSU process: standby RP upgraded first, switchover (SSO), active RP upgraded, switchover back. Throughout: NSF maintains forwarding, SSO maintains protocol states. Requires: SSO configured, NSF for OSPF/BGP/EIGRP, ISSU-capable hardware, compatible versions.

questions.question: What is Cisco DNA Spaces and location services integration?
options: A cloud platform using Wi-Fi infrastructure for indoor location services — tracks connected devices, provides analytics on foot traffic, dwell time, presence detection, integrates with retail/healthcare/workplace applications
questions.explanation: DNA Spaces: uses Cisco AP RSSI data for location. REST APIs for app integration. Use cases: retail analytics (dwell time, path analysis), hospital asset tracking, workplace occupancy. Requires Catalyst Center + CMX license or DNA Spaces subscription.
